job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Liam Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm up at seven because my dad is, and he's an electrician, so the house wakes early. I live with my parents in a small town outside Leicester. I finished electrical engineering in the summer with a pass. My final project was a control board for a solar inverter, which actually worked in the lab, but nobody saw it outside the lab. I do applications at the dining table, then walk to the hardware shop where my uncle lets me stack shelves for a few hours so I'm not just sitting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work do you actually enjoy?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I don't have internships. I did a week of site shadowing with my dad's friend, but that's not on any form. I'm not good at selling myself, to be honest. I'd rather someone just looked at my project and said fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's the sensible outcome. Most hype dies down and the grid still needs people who understand voltage. I'd say that to my dad, who'd say he told me so. I wouldn't write anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan hasn't changed. Apply to the energy companies, the network operators and the contractors, and wait for someone to call. There are plenty of openings in the area, but my CV has nothing on it besides a pass. I'm not worried about money, my parents have always saved. I'm worried about being forgotten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep posting applications, about ten a week, mainly to the electricity network and to two contractors that my dad knows. I'd ring each one after a week, which I hate doing. I'd work the shop shifts and finish a second small project, a battery charging controller. I still wouldn't use any AI tool; I'd write my own cover letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, I guess. Nothing dramatic, just a quiet kind of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hate ringing firms after a week. What's hard about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel like I'm bothering them. My dad says that's how work gets done, you ring and you show up. I wrote a short script in my notebook, which sounds silly, but it helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not use an AI tool for cover letters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust it to sound like me, and I don't like not knowing where the words came from. Maybe that's old-fashioned. I'd rather write a plain letter badly than a clever one I can't explain.

say: I'd say it's the **sensible** outcome: the grid still needs people who understand voltage.
I'd tell my dad he was right and write nothing online.
think: My plan stays the same: apply and **wait** for someone to call.
I'm not worried about money; I'm worried about **being forgotten**.
do: Post **ten applications a week** to the network operator and two contractors my dad knows.
Finish a second project, a **battery charging controller**, and ring each firm after a week.
S0.quote: I'm not worried about money, my parents have always saved. I'm worried about being forgotten.
fieldNote: Fear of being **forgotten** matters more to him than money.
Dislikes **selling** himself and uses a notebook script for calls.
Refuses AI because he wants to **explain** every word he sends.

steps.text: Post ten applications a week to the network operator and two contractors
Finish a battery charging controller as a second project

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds like office work will change and the grid will carry on much the same. Planning, drawing and checking can be done by software, but a substation still needs a person with a torch. I'd say that at dinner and my dad would nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it affects the design side of electrical engineering first. Drawing schematics, running load calculations, writing reports. Those are the jobs I'd be applying to as a graduate. The site and maintenance work moves more slowly, which suits me, though it means I'd have to do the muddy part first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift the applications towards site and maintenance roles at the network operator, even on a lower wage. I'd sign up for the apprenticeship-style scheme if one exists. I'd also ask my dad whether I can ride along on his jobs on Saturdays and learn the real trade. I'd still be slow on the AI tools; maybe I'd watch a colleague use one for a month before I try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for me yet, but for other graduates who are better at drawing than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ride along with your dad. What would you learn there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How houses are actually wired, which a degree skips. Dad can look at a fuse box and tell you which cowboy did it. That kind of knowledge isn't on any slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The designers in the back office, people like my cousin Hanna, who does drawings all day. If software does the first draft, I can't see why they'd keep as many. I'd feel for her, and I'd be afraid to say it.

say: I'd say the **grid** carries on the same, since a substation still needs a person with a torch.
I'd say it at dinner, where my dad would nod.
think: The **design side** goes first: schematics, load calculations and reports.
Site and maintenance work moves slowly, which suits me, though I'd do the **muddy part** first.
do: Apply for **site and maintenance** roles at the network operator, even at lower pay.
Ride along on my **dad's Saturday jobs** to learn the real trade.
feel: **Uneasy** for others better at drawing than me, but not for myself yet.
S1.quote: Dad can look at a fuse box and tell you which cowboy did it. That kind of knowledge isn't on any slide.
fieldNote: Reads **design** work as exposed and site work as safer, which is accurate for his field.
Worry is about **others**, such as his cousin, more than himself.
Won't touch AI until he has watched a **colleague** use it.

steps.text: Apply for site and maintenance roles at the network operator
Ride along on my dad's Saturday jobs to learn domestic wiring
Keep stacking shelves at the hardware shop while I wait

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to cope with. I'd say, hang on, who decided this? I'd also say my dad's trade is safer than my degree for a few years. I'd feel awkward saying that to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it would scare me. By 2028, a graduate electrical engineer whose job is to draw and calculate is easy to replace. Robots that can do hands-on work like my dad's would come about 2031, and after that even the trade isn't safe. So the whole thing has a clock on it. I'm resistant to change, and now it's change or be left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job, including a site assistant role. I'd ask my dad to teach me everything I could about domestic and small commercial work. I'd put my savings in the bank and not touch them, and I'd skip the holiday I was planning with my cousin. I'd reluctantly try one AI tool just to see what it's doing to people's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like standing on a platform and the train is early. I'd be thinking about it on the bus and in the shower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel awkward telling your dad his trade is safer. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad is proud of my degree, he told the whole street. If I say it's the wrong bet, it feels like I'm wasting his pride. I'd probably say it in the van, where nobody's looking at each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the savings you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. They'd sit there. I'd want to have six months in the bank before any decision. If the economy went strange I want to be the one who doesn't need a loan.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for anyone to cope with and ask who decided it.
I'd awkwardly admit my dad's trade is safer than my degree.
think: By 2028 a graduate who draws and calculates is **easy to replace**.
Robots arrive around 2031, so even my dad's trade has a **clock** on it.
do: Take **any job**, even site assistant, and learn domestic wiring from my dad.
Leave savings **untouched** and skip the holiday with my cousin.
feel: **Anxious**, like standing on a platform when the train is early.
S2.quote: My dad is proud of my degree, he told the whole street. If I say it's the wrong bet, it feels like I'm wasting his pride.
fieldNote: Fear is tied to his **father's pride**, not only to income.
His resistance to change turns into **forced** change.
Unlikely to spend savings; wants a **buffer** before decisions.

steps.text: Take any job offered, including site assistant work
Keep savings untouched and aim for six months in the bank
Skip the holiday with my cousin and cut extra spending
Try one AI tool once to see what it does to work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to see which trades and companies are really changing. I'd tell my friends not to panic, but not to just sit and wait either. I'd say we should talk to our local councillor about what happens to apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel worried, but I'd have a bit of room. Five years is enough to get a first job, get a qualification and become someone people know. By 2031 the design office work has probably moved to AI. Robots for hands-on work around 2034 give me about three extra years if I'm on site. I'd say my job is whatever is on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a contractor job in the first six months and ask them to sponsor me for chartership. I'd do the courses in the evenings, though I'd hate it. I'd save at least 400 a month and put it in a tracker fund my dad trusts. And I'd keep learning how the grid works, so I understand what I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than the two-year one. At least I could picture the next few steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save in a tracker fund your dad trusts. How does that decision get made?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's investment is simple: put money in something broad and leave it. I don't like complicated products. If I can't explain an investment at the pub, I'm not buying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your local councillor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the apprenticeship schemes will survive and whether someone checks that the firms actually train people. Ten years ago there was a scheme that turned out to be cheap labour. I'd want a real inspection.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to see which **trades** really change.
I'd urge my friends to talk to our local councillor about **apprentices**.
think: The design office work probably moves to AI by **2031**.
On site I'd get about **three extra years** before robots arrive.
do: Get a **contractor job** in six months and ask them to sponsor my chartership.
Save **400 a month** in a broad tracker fund my dad trusts.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier because I can picture the next steps.
S3.quote: If I can't explain an investment at the pub, I'm not buying it.
fieldNote: Plans stay **concrete** and low-risk, matching his resistant style.
Distrusts **schemes** after seeing an apprenticeship turn into cheap labour.
Sees **site work** as his safest ground.

steps.text: Take a contractor job and ask them to sponsor my chartership
Do the chartership courses in the evenings for two years
Save 400 a month from my first pay cheque
Put savings in a broad tracker fund my dad trusts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and anyone who's panicking is wasting it. I'd say the sensible thing is to do your job well and see. At home I'd say I'll be thirty-three and probably fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I'd feel mostly okay. A decade is plenty for a first job, a proper qualification and maybe a team to lead. Robots for hands-on work around 2039 means my dad's trade will last my working years, I'd guess. I worry a little about my own children, if I have any, but that's far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'd do anyway: get any entry job at the network operator, qualify, and save. Maybe I'd buy a small flat in my late twenties. I'd also pick up one AI tool when it's clearly part of the job, because my future boss would want it. Until then I'd stick to what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I'd still check the news now and then, but I'd treat it like weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pick up AI when it's clearly part of the job. How would you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the training department puts it in a course, or when my manager asks for it. I'm not against AI tools. I just want the instruction to come from someone who's accountable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'fine' look like at thirty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A steady engineering job, a flat with a garden my dad can complain about, and enough put away for a wedding. If my mum can stop worrying about me, that's a win.

say: I'd say **panicking** over ten years wastes the time.
I'd say the sensible thing is to do your job well and see.
think: A decade is plenty for a first job, a **qualification** and maybe a team.
My dad's trade should last my **working years**.
do: Take any **entry job** at the network operator, qualify and save.
Buy a small **flat** in my late twenties.
feel: **Fairly calm**: I'd treat the news like weather.
S4.quote: I'm not against AI tools. I just want the instruction to come from someone who's accountable.
fieldNote: He describes a **steady** life as the goal, which fits his outlook.
His AI stance is about **accountability**, not fear.
Long horizon pushes worries toward **future children**.

steps.text: Take an entry job at the network operator and finish my qualification
Complete the chartership courses over three years
Save for a small flat deposit by my late twenties
Plan the flat and a wedding fund with my family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. It's too quick for someone like me, who needs time to get used to things. What would help is a clear route into a trade, with real training and a real wage, and someone who checks that it isn't just cheap labour.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say this. Not everyone is loud about their fears. People like me just get on with it and keep quiet. That doesn't mean we aren't scared.

headlineQuote: Not everyone is loud about their fears. People like me just get on with it and keep quiet.
portrait: Liam is **23**, an electrical engineering graduate with a pass, living with his parents near Leicester and stacking shelves for his uncle.
He prefers the **familiar**, never uses AI, and wants proof from a trusted colleague before trying any tool.
His father is an electrician, so he sees **site work** as his safety net and the design office as the risk.
He is centrist, blames **no one** loudly, and keeps his fears quiet, which hides how anxious he can get.
His mood moves from calm in the plateau to **anxious** in the 2028 and 2031 pictures, then settles with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most because he needs time to get used to change.
whatWouldHelp: A clear route into a **trade**, with real training and a real wage, checked so it isn't cheap labour.
